messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 20
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Soldier
  trauma_type: Assault
  pcl5: 33

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Overeating: I eat more than usual to distract myself or feel better, Redirection: I think of something else, Overanalysing: I go over and over the details of the event trying to make sense of it
  Memory: Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me, Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
  Negative Appraisals: Others-Would-Cope: Somebody else would have stopped the event from happening, Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture, Unrecognisable Self: The person I have become is unrecognisable to me

Vignette:
Linh Tran is a twenty-year-old Vietnamese American soldier, married and currently stationed at a domestic base, who was referred for psychological evaluation following a disclosed assault that occurred approximately seven months ago. She presented to the intake session as guarded but cooperative, speaking quietly and with frequent pauses, as though choosing each word with care.

The assault took place during an off-duty evening on base. Linh had stayed late in a common area after a unit social event when a fellow service member cornered her in a corridor. What followed was a physical and sexual assault that lasted several minutes before she was able to leave. Throughout the assault, Linh had been acutely aware of the fluorescent light buzzing overhead, the particular smell of the cleaning solution used in that hallway, and the sound of distant music still playing from the room she had just left. She did not call out. She did not fight back as forcefully as she later felt she should have. She walked back to her quarters, showered, and told no one for three weeks.

In the months that followed, Linh noticed that her memory of the event had a quality she struggled to articulate. She described it as watching footage of a stranger — she could recall the images with uncomfortable clarity, the visual details sharp and sequential, and yet she had come to feel that the person in those images could not really be her. The memory was so extreme, so far outside anything she had imagined her life could contain, that there were moments she genuinely doubted it had happened to her at all. She found herself going over and over the details in the evenings, trying to construct a version of events that made logical sense, searching for the precise moment things could have gone differently. What she kept arriving at was the certainty that someone else — someone stronger, more alert, less frozen — would have stopped it from happening. That conviction had settled into something firm and self-condemning.

Linh's daily life as a soldier placed her in close proximity to the building where the assault occurred. She passed the corridor entrance during routine movement between facilities several times a week. On those occasions, the fluorescent lighting and the faint chemical smell of institutional cleaner were enough to pull her back into the visual memory with an immediacy she found disorienting. She had begun taking a longer route between buildings, adding nearly ten minutes to her daily movements, and had not re-entered that corridor since the night of the assault. Her supervisor had noticed the routing change and made an offhand comment about it; Linh had offered no explanation.

At home, her husband, Minh, had noticed she was eating differently — larger portions, snacking late into the night, reaching for food at moments that had no obvious connection to hunger. When the images came or when the mental replaying began, eating was something to do with her body, a way of occupying herself that temporarily interrupted the loop. Linh was aware that she was doing it and felt some shame about it, though she had not connected it to the assault in any conversation with Minh. She had also developed a habit of redirecting her thoughts mid-sentence — changing the subject internally, reaching for something neutral whenever the corridor or the evening began to surface.

What had changed most quietly, and most painfully, was her sense of belonging. Linh had grown up in a tight Vietnamese American community in which her decision to enlist had already created some distance. The assault had deepened that distance into something she could no longer name. She did not attend the Tết gathering her mother-in-law organised in February. She felt, without being able to fully explain it, that she no longer fit anywhere she used to fit — not in her family's world, not in the unit's camaraderie, not in her own sense of who she was before that evening. The person she caught herself being — avoidant, hollow, unrecognisable — was not someone she had any framework for.

What finally brought Linh to seek help was a conversation with Minh in which he told her, gently, that he felt he was losing her. She did not want to lose him too. What she feared most, sitting in the intake room, was that the person she had been before was simply gone.
